question: A broker sponsors a five-person sales team branded 'The Summit Group' in all yard signs, digital ads, and business cards, none of which display the sponsoring broker's name. The team's unlicensed marketing coordinator regularly fields buyer calls generated by these ads and discusses listing price flexibility and possible offer terms with prospective buyers before referring them to a licensed team member. This combination of practices most clearly violates:
choice_a: Both TREC's advertising rules requiring the sponsoring broker's name to appear in team advertising and the prohibition on an unlicensed person performing acts that require a license, such as discussing negotiable contract terms with a prospective buyer
choice_b: Only the advertising rule, since discussing price flexibility with a caller is not itself a licensed activity
choice_c: Neither practice, since team branding and using support staff to field initial calls are both fully permissible without restriction
choice_d: Only the unlicensed-activity concern, since a broker-sponsored team is never required to disclose the sponsoring broker's name in its advertising
explanation: Team advertising must include the sponsoring broker's name under TREC's advertising rule, and clerical/administrative support staff who are not licensed may not discuss negotiable terms, price flexibility, or other substantive matters that constitute performing an act requiring a real estate license -- the coordinator's role here crosses well past permitted scheduling/clerical functions into unlicensed brokerage activity, compounding the office's separate advertising defect.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.155 (Advertisements); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Appropriate Use of Unlicensed Assistants) and VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker owns a minority ownership interest in a title company and, consistent with RESPA's affiliated business arrangement exception, gives the buyer a proper written disclosure at referral, confirms use of the title company is optional, and receives only a return on ownership rather than a referral fee. Unrelated to the title company, the same broker also personally owns the moving company the broker recommends to the buyer for the move-in, without ever mentioning that ownership interest to the buyer. This combination shows that:
choice_a: Complying with RESPA's affiliated business arrangement disclosure requirements for the title company referral does not excuse the broker from the separate, broader state-law fiduciary duty to disclose a personal financial interest in the moving company recommendation, since RESPA's disclosure rules apply specifically to settlement services, not to every referral a broker makes
choice_b: No further disclosure is required for the moving company, since RESPA compliance for the title company referral covers all of the broker's business referrals in the same transaction
choice_c: The moving company referral is not a real estate matter and is therefore entirely outside any Texas licensing concern
choice_d: The broker's ownership interest in the title company creates a violation regardless of the proper RESPA disclosure, since brokers may never hold any ownership interest in a settlement service provider
explanation: RESPA's affiliated business arrangement exception, when its written-disclosure, no-required-use, and bona-fide-compensation conditions are satisfied, lawfully permits a broker's ownership interest in a settlement service provider like a title company -- but that federal disclosure obligation is narrow, tied specifically to settlement services covered by RESPA. It does not substitute for TREC's own, broader fiduciary duty requiring a license holder to disclose any personal or financial interest the license holder holds in a business recommended to a client, including businesses (like a moving company) that fall outside RESPA's settlement-service scope entirely.
source_note: RESPA Section 8 affiliated business arrangement exception (12 U.S.C. Section 2607(c)(4)); Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.652(b) and 22 TAC Section 531.3 (Integrity) disclosure-of-interest principles; Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's property management client's tenant vacates a rental home on the 1st of the month, promptly returns keys, and provides a forwarding address. The broker's bookkeeper is on leave, and on day 35 the broker still has not sent the tenant any refund or itemized deduction statement, though the trust ledger for that unit is accurately reconciled and the funds remain properly held. This scenario illustrates that:
choice_a: Properly holding and reconciling a tenant's security deposit in the broker's trust account satisfies trust-fund handling rules, but does not by itself satisfy the landlord's separate statutory duty under Property Code Chapter 92 to refund the deposit (or provide an itemized list of any deductions) within 30 days of surrender, a deadline the broker, acting as the owner's agent, must also track and meet
choice_b: No deadline applies as long as the broker's trust account records are accurate and the deposit itself was never mishandled
choice_c: Only the property owner, never the managing broker, can be responsible for a late security deposit accounting under Texas law
choice_d: The broker has 30 additional days beyond the standard deadline whenever the bookkeeper is unavailable
explanation: Trust account recordkeeping accuracy under 22 TAC Section 535.146 and the landlord's independent statutory deadline to refund a tenant's security deposit (or provide an itemized deduction list) within 30 days of surrender under Property Code Sections 92.103-92.104 are two distinct obligations -- a broker acting as the owner's property manager must satisfy both, and internal staffing issues do not extend the statutory deadline, which can expose the owner (and, through the management relationship, the broker) to statutory penalties including forfeiture of the right to withhold any portion of the deposit.
source_note: Texas Property Code Sections 92.103-92.104 (Security Deposits); 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker decides to close their brokerage and retire. At the time of closing, the trust account holds earnest money for two pending sales and security deposits for four active rental properties, and six sales agents are still sponsored under the firm. Properly winding down requires the broker to:
choice_a: Simultaneously address multiple distinct obligations -- properly disbursing or transferring all trust account funds only as the rules and any principals' agreements allow, ensuring each sponsored agent's sponsorship is timely and properly terminated or transferred with TREC, and giving clients with open transactions or active management agreements adequate notice and a clear path forward
choice_b: Simply lock the office and stop responding to calls, since a retiring broker has no further obligations once the decision to close is made
choice_c: Keep the trust account open and funded indefinitely under the broker's now-inactive license, since closing a brokerage automatically extends all trust duties
choice_d: Transfer all trust funds directly into the broker's personal account for safekeeping until each matter resolves
explanation: Winding down a brokerage is not a single action but a set of parallel obligations -- trust money must be properly resolved consistent with 22 TAC Section 535.146 (never simply moved to a personal account), sponsored agents' licenses must be properly transferred or terminated with TREC so they are not left in supervisory limbo, and clients with pending transactions or management agreements need timely notice so their interests are protected; neglecting any one of these threads while focusing only on another leaves both clients and the broker exposed.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money -- closing a brokerage); 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- sponsorship); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A brother sells his half-interest in an inherited house directly to his sister, who already co-owns the other half -- a transfer between co-owners that is exempt from the Property Code's Seller's Disclosure Notice requirement. The brother knows the home has an active, undisclosed slab leak he never mentioned to his sister before she paid him for his interest. The disclosure exemption for this transfer means:
choice_a: The brother is not required to complete the statutory Seller's Disclosure Notice form for this transfer, but the exemption from that specific form does not shield him from potential fraud or misrepresentation liability for knowingly failing to disclose a material latent defect he was aware of
choice_b: The brother has no disclosure-related exposure whatsoever, since the exemption from the Seller's Disclosure Notice covers all disclosure obligations of any kind
choice_c: The exemption applies only if the sister is also a licensed real estate agent
choice_d: The transfer is automatically voidable the moment any statutory exemption applies, regardless of what either party knew
explanation: Property Code Section 5.008(b) exempts certain transfers, including those between co-owners, from the specific statutory Seller's Disclosure Notice requirement -- but that narrow exemption only removes the obligation to complete that particular form. It does not eliminate the independent, broader common-law and TRELA prohibition on knowingly concealing a material defect from the other party to a transaction, which can still expose the brother to a fraud or misrepresentation claim.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008 (Seller Disclosure Requirements -- exemptions); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A seller signs a flat-fee, limited-service listing agreement under which the broker's only promised service is placing the listing on the MLS; the agreement includes a clause stating the seller 'waives the broker's obligation to forward any offer directly to the seller.' A buyer submits a written offer directly to the broker. The broker's correct action, despite the waiver clause, is to:
choice_a: Forward the written offer to the seller anyway, since Texas's minimum-services requirements obligate a broker to at least accept and forward offers and counteroffers to the client regardless of a limited-service agreement's terms, and a private waiver clause cannot lawfully eliminate that baseline duty
choice_b: Honor the waiver clause exactly as written and simply discard the offer without telling the seller
choice_c: Forward the offer only if the seller specifically calls to ask whether any offers have come in
choice_d: Treat the waiver as valid because sellers are always free to contractually eliminate any brokerage duty they choose
explanation: Texas's minimum-services statute sets a floor of duties -- including submitting all offers and counteroffers to the client -- that a limited-service listing agreement cannot waive away, even with an express clause purporting to do so; a broker who honors such an unenforceable waiver and withholds a written offer from the seller has violated the statute regardless of what the listing agreement says.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.5545 (Minimum Services); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A Texas broker receives a referral of a relocating buyer from a broker licensed only in Colorado, who has no Texas license and performs no negotiation activity within Texas. Separately, an unlicensed friend of the Texas broker's client mentioned the broker's services to the buyer over coffee, with no other involvement. At closing, the Texas broker wants to pay a referral fee to both the Colorado broker and the friend. This is:
choice_a: Permissible only as to the Colorado broker, since Texas law allows paying a commission to a broker licensed in another state under specified conditions such as not conducting negotiations within Texas, but paying any fee to the unlicensed friend for the referral would violate the prohibition on compensating unlicensed persons for an act requiring a license
choice_b: Permissible as to both, since any referral that produces a paying client may be lawfully compensated regardless of licensing status
choice_c: Impermissible as to both, since Texas brokers may never pay compensation to anyone outside their own sponsored sales agents
choice_d: Permissible only as to the unlicensed friend, since casual personal referrals are exempt from licensing requirements while broker-to-broker payments always require a Texas license
explanation: Texas law permits a broker to pay compensation to a real estate broker licensed only in another state under specified conditions, including that the non-resident broker not conduct negotiations for the transaction within Texas -- but that accommodation for licensed non-resident brokers does not extend to unlicensed individuals; paying anyone, including a client's friend, for making a referral that amounts to performing an act requiring a license remains prohibited.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.651 (Compensation for Performing Brokerage Activities); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: Intermediary broker Elena has appointed agent Ray to the buyer and appointed agent Priya to the seller in the same transaction. Ray proactively sends detailed updates on his buyer's situation to Elena's office almost daily, while Priya, dealing with a slower-moving seller, checks in far less often. A review of Elena's file notes shows meaningfully more documented contact with the buyer's side than the seller's side by closing. Standing alone, this disparity in contact volume:
choice_a: Does not, by itself, establish a violation of the intermediary's duty to act fairly and impartially, since that duty is satisfied by complying with the statute's specific requirements -- such as not disclosing certain confidential information without consent and treating both parties honestly -- not by guaranteeing identical volumes of communication regardless of each side's own pace and responsiveness
choice_b: Automatically proves Elena violated her duty of impartiality, since equal contact minutes with each side is legally mandatory
choice_c: Is irrelevant because intermediary brokers owe no duty of fairness to either appointed party once agents are appointed
choice_d: Means Ray, not Elena, is solely responsible for any resulting fairness complaint, since Elena delegated contact to the appointed agents
explanation: TRELA Section 1101.559(c)'s 'fair and impartial' standard is satisfied through compliance with the statute's specific substantive requirements -- honest treatment, accurate information, and not disclosing information the other party asked to keep confidential without consent -- not through an artificial requirement that every appointed agent generate identical volumes of contact regardless of how responsive each party's own side actually is; differences driven by the parties' own pace are not, without more, evidence of favoritism.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559(c) (Broker Acting as Intermediary -- fair and impartial standard); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker reviewing a closed file discovers that a sponsored sales agent signed an exclusive listing agreement in the agent's own name rather than the sponsoring broker's name, and that earnest money was later collected and properly deposited into the brokerage's trust account once a buyer was found. The broker's review should treat this as:
choice_a: Two separate issues requiring two separate responses -- correcting the agent's improper practice of contracting in the agent's own name rather than the broker's, since a sponsored agent's authority to enter listing and representation agreements runs through the broker, while recognizing that the earnest money itself, once actually received by the brokerage, was still properly handled as trust money regardless of the earlier contracting defect
choice_b: A single non-issue, since any earnest money that ends up properly deposited automatically cures any defect in how the underlying listing agreement was signed
choice_c: Grounds to treat the listing agreement, and every later step in the transaction including the trust deposit, as entirely void from the outset
choice_d: Solely a trust account problem, with no concern at all regarding whose name appears on the listing agreement
explanation: A sponsored sales agent generally must enter listing and representation agreements in the sponsoring broker's name, since the agent acts as the broker's representative rather than as an independent contracting party -- that defect is a real compliance issue the broker must correct going forward, even though it is analytically separate from the trust account question of whether the earnest money, once actually collected, was properly deposited and accounted for.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A seller instructs listing agent Wen to tell any prospective buyers who 'sound foreign' that the home is already under contract, even when it is not, hoping to discourage certain buyers from making offers. Wen refuses to make any such misrepresentation to any buyer. The seller is angry and insists Wen follow instructions or be fired as the listing agent. Wen's correct understanding of agency law here is that:
choice_a: An agent's duty of obedience extends only to the client's lawful instructions; Wen must decline any instruction that would require fair-housing discrimination or an affirmative misrepresentation to third parties, and if the seller will not relent, Wen may need to end the representation rather than comply, consistent with any termination terms in the listing agreement
choice_b: Wen must follow the seller's instruction regardless of its content, since the duty of obedience to a client is absolute and overrides all other legal considerations
choice_c: Wen's only lawful option is to continue representing the seller exactly as instructed while privately telling buyers the truth behind the seller's back
choice_d: Refusing the seller's instruction is itself a breach of fiduciary duty to the client
explanation: The agency duty of obedience is a duty to follow a client's lawful instructions -- it does not require, or even permit, an agent to comply with an instruction that would violate fair housing law or require an affirmative misrepresentation to a third party. An agent who properly refuses such an instruction has not breached any duty to the client; if the client will not accept that limit, ending the representation according to the agreement's terms is the appropriate path, not silent noncompliance while continuing to represent the seller as if nothing happened.
source_note: National/General Broker Content Outline V.C (Fair Housing) and V.B.1 (agency duties -- obedience limited to lawful instructions); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A failed transaction leaves $8,000 in earnest money in a broker's trust account. The seller wants the funds; the buyer disputes that any default occurred. A sales agent, hoping to quickly resolve the dispute and preserve the office's relationship with the seller, signs the buyer's name on a Release of Earnest Money form without the buyer's knowledge or authorization, and the broker disburses the funds to the seller based on that document. This scenario reflects:
choice_a: Two distinct and serious violations layered together -- the agent's forgery of the buyer's signature is a separate act of document fraud exposing the agent, and potentially the broker given supervisory responsibility, and the broker's disbursement was improper because a valid release requires actual, authorized consent from both principals, which never existed here
choice_b: A single, relatively minor paperwork issue, since the seller was arguably entitled to the funds under the facts regardless of how the release was obtained
choice_c: No violation at all, as long as the broker genuinely believed in good faith that the buyer would have agreed if asked
choice_d: A violation attributable solely to the agent, with no possible supervisory exposure for the broker under any circumstances
explanation: A broker may not disburse disputed trust funds without genuine, authorized consent from both principals (or another lawful basis such as a court order); a forged signature never satisfies that requirement and independently constitutes a serious act of document fraud, layering a forgery violation on top of an improper, unauthorized trust fund disbursement -- and the broker's own supervisory responsibility for the agent's conduct remains squarely in play.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.652(b)(31) (improper trust fund disbursement); 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money); 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker, without engaging a licensed auctioneer, markets an upcoming listed-property event as a 'no-reserve auction,' telling prospective bidders in writing that 'the property will sell to the highest bidder no matter what, with absolutely no minimum price.' Behind the scenes, the seller has privately instructed the broker that he will not accept less than $250,000. This arrangement raises which concern under Texas advertising and licensing standards?
choice_a: The advertised 'no minimum' representation is misleading if the seller has actually reserved a minimum acceptable price, since advertising and promotional materials must accurately reflect the actual terms of the sale being offered to the public
choice_b: No concern exists as long as the broker eventually discloses the reserve price after the auction concludes
choice_c: The advertisement is proper because sellers are legally required to accept any bid regardless of amount once an advertised auction begins
choice_d: The concern applies only to licensed auctioneers, never to a real estate broker marketing the broker's own listing
explanation: TREC advertising standards require that marketing accurately reflect the actual terms being offered; representing a sale as an unconditional 'no minimum, sells no matter what' auction while the seller has privately set a reserve price the broker knows about is a misleading representation -- a broker cannot use auction-style marketing to create a false impression of the actual sale terms, regardless of whatever separate licensing framework may govern professional auctioneers generally.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.155 (Advertisements); Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.652(b)(17) (misleading representations); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: Sales agent Marcus, sponsored by ABC Realty, is representing a buyer under a buyer representation agreement. Midway through the buyer's search, Marcus discovers the home the buyer wants to write an offer on is actually listed by another agent at ABC Realty, a fact neither agent had realized until now. Before Marcus's buyer submits an offer on that specific listing, the correct next step is to:
choice_a: Recognize that ABC Realty's brokerage now represents both the buyer and the seller in the same transaction, requiring the broker to obtain both parties' written consent to intermediary status (with appropriate appointments, if used) before the transaction proceeds any further
choice_b: Do nothing differently, since Marcus and the listing agent work independently and the shared brokerage affiliation has no legal significance
choice_c: Have Marcus simply stop representing the buyer entirely with no further action needed, since any brokerage-level conflict automatically resolves itself once one agent withdraws
choice_d: Proceed with the offer as planned, and address the shared-brokerage issue only if a dispute later arises
explanation: Because both the buyer and the seller are represented by license holders sponsored by the same brokerage, the broker -- not just the individual agents -- represents both parties to this transaction, triggering the same written-consent-to-intermediary requirement that applies to any dual representation, even though neither agent set out to create that situation; the transaction should not proceed further on this specific property until proper consent, and appointments if used, are in place.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559 (Broker Acting as Intermediary); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A sponsored sales agent lets her license lapse into inactive status by failing to complete required continuing education, but continues showing properties, submitting offers, and collecting commission checks with the broker's knowledge for several more weeks because 'the paperwork is just a formality.' The broker's exposure here includes:
choice_a: Both the agent's own unlicensed practice, since an inactive license does not authorize performing acts that require an active license, and the broker's separate supervisory failure to verify and maintain awareness of each sponsored agent's actual license status before allowing continued activity
choice_b: No exposure for either party, since the agent's license was active as recently as a few weeks earlier
choice_c: Exposure for the agent alone, since a sponsoring broker has no duty to monitor a sponsored agent's ongoing license status once initially verified at hiring
choice_d: Exposure only if a client specifically complains about the agent's license status
explanation: An inactive real estate license does not authorize performing any act requiring an active license -- continuing to show property, negotiate, or earn commissions on inactive status is unlicensed activity -- and a sponsoring broker's ongoing supervisory duty includes maintaining awareness of each sponsored agent's actual, current license status, not simply verifying it once when sponsorship begins.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Chapter 1101 (active license status requirements); 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker's unlicensed marketing assistant hosts a Sunday open house alone while the sponsored listing agent is unavailable. A visitor asks the assistant whether the seller would consider $15,000 under asking price, and the assistant responds, 'Honestly, I think they'd take it -- they're pretty motivated.' The broker later learns of this exchange. This is problematic because:
choice_a: Discussing the seller's likely willingness to negotiate price is well outside the ministerial, clerical tasks an unlicensed assistant may lawfully perform unsupervised, and it exposes the broker to both an unlicensed-practice concern and potential liability if the assistant's unauthorized, unverified comment turns out to be inaccurate or is treated as authoritative by the visitor
choice_b: There is no issue, since greeting visitors at an open house is always an acceptable unlicensed task regardless of what is discussed once there
choice_c: The only concern is that the assistant should have first gotten the seller's permission to speak at all, not the substance of what was said
choice_d: This exposes only the assistant to any consequence, since the broker was not present when the comment was made
explanation: An unlicensed assistant may perform ministerial and clerical tasks such as greeting visitors and distributing materials, but speculating about a seller's negotiating flexibility is a substantive, negotiation-adjacent statement that only a licensed and properly informed license holder should make -- this crosses from permitted clerical support into unlicensed practice, and a broker's supervisory responsibility for what happens at broker-sponsored marketing events does not evaporate simply because the broker was not personally present.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Appropriate Use of Unlicensed Assistants); 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A seller's written Seller's Disclosure Notice accurately states 'Unknown' in response to the flooding history question, since the seller genuinely does not know whether the home has ever flooded. During a showing, the seller's own agent, wanting to reassure a hesitant buyer, tells the buyer verbally, 'Don't worry, this house has never flooded.' The buyer later discovers it flooded twice under a prior owner. In this situation:
choice_a: The seller's written disclosure was lawful and accurate as an honest 'Unknown' answer, but the agent's own affirmative verbal statement went beyond what the seller actually knew or disclosed and independently exposes the agent to misrepresentation liability, separate from whatever the seller's compliant written disclosure said
choice_b: Neither the seller nor the agent has any exposure, since the written disclosure form is the only document that legally matters
choice_c: The agent is fully protected from liability because the agent was merely repeating information consistent with the seller's own disclosure form
choice_d: Only the seller can be held responsible for the agent's verbal statement, since agents cannot be independently liable for misrepresentation
explanation: Answering 'Unknown' on a Seller's Disclosure Notice is a lawful, accurate response when the seller genuinely lacks the information -- but an agent who then affirmatively and specifically asserts a fact the agent does not actually know to be true, here flatly promising the home 'has never flooded,' creates independent misrepresentation exposure for the agent personally, since that statement goes well beyond, and actually contradicts, what the seller's own accurate disclosure said.
source_note: Texas Property Code Section 5.008 (Seller Disclosure Requirements); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies); National/General Broker Content Outline V.D.5 (fraud and misrepresentation)

question: A buyer's contract for a home in a mandatory-membership HOA subdivision includes the TREC addendum for property subject to a property owners' association. The seller's HOA is slow to respond, and the subdivision information/resale certificate required under Texas Property Code Chapter 207 is not delivered to the buyer before closing is scheduled. The broker's correct advice to the buyer is that:
choice_a: Because the required subdivision information was not timely delivered, the buyer generally has a statutory right to terminate the contract for any reason within a short window after actually receiving it, or before closing, whichever comes first, and the broker should help the buyer track that deadline rather than assume the sale must simply proceed or die
choice_b: The buyer has no recourse and must either close without the information or forfeit the earnest money
choice_c: The HOA's delay automatically voids the entire contract with no action required by either party
choice_d: Only the seller, not the buyer, has any termination right connected to late delivery of subdivision information
explanation: Texas Property Code Chapter 207 and the TREC property owners' association addendum give a purchaser in a mandatory-membership property owners' association a right to terminate the contract for any reason within a limited period after actually receiving the required subdivision information, or before closing, whichever occurs first, if it was not delivered by the contractual deadline -- this is a purchaser protection the broker must actively track and advise on, not an automatic contract-voiding event or a dead end requiring the buyer to simply close or lose their deposit.
source_note: Texas Property Code Chapter 207 (Texas Residential Property Owners Protection Act -- subdivision information/resale certificate); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline V.A (Promulgated Contracts, Forms, and Addenda) and VII (Case Studies)

question: Two days before a scheduled closing, a broker's bookkeeper discovers the brokerage's trust account is $1,400 short of the total owed to principals across several open files, apparently due to a bank fee mistakenly charged against the trust account months earlier. One of the shortfall's affected files is the transaction closing in two days. The broker's correct sequence of action is to:
choice_a: Immediately identify and cure the shortage -- promptly depositing sufficient funds from the broker's own resources if needed -- and fully reconcile the account before relying on it to fund any closing disbursement, rather than allowing the closing to proceed on the assumption the account will simply work itself out
choice_b: Proceed with the closing as scheduled and address the shortage sometime afterward, since the amount involved is relatively small
choice_c: Delay the closing indefinitely with no communication to the parties until the broker personally has time to investigate
choice_d: Cover the shortfall by temporarily using a different file's trust funds until the bank fee issue is sorted out
explanation: A trust account shortage, regardless of its cause, must be identified and cured promptly, including the broker covering the gap from the broker's own funds if necessary, and the account must be fully reconciled before the broker relies on it to fund a disbursement; proceeding with a closing while a known shortfall sits uncorrected risks an improper disbursement, and using one client's funds to patch another's shortfall is commingling and misapplication, not a permissible fix.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money); Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.652(b)(31); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A broker who owns two offices in different cities designates the office manager at the satellite location, who is a licensed broker, to handle periodic supervisory file reviews there, and does not personally check in on that office's compliance for several months. During that time, an agent at the satellite office is found to have mishandled client trust funds, a problem the office manager never caught because the promised periodic reviews were not being consistently performed. The designating broker's responsibility here is:
choice_a: Not eliminated by the delegation -- while a broker may delegate supervisory tasks to another qualified license holder, the broker retains ultimate responsibility for ensuring adequate supervision actually occurs at every location the broker operates, and simply assigning the task without ever confirming it was being carried out does not satisfy that responsibility
choice_b: Fully eliminated once supervisory tasks are delegated to any other licensed broker, regardless of whether the delegated tasks were ever actually performed
choice_c: Limited entirely to the satellite office's manager, since the designating broker never personally worked at that location
choice_d: Nonexistent, since only the individual agent who mishandled funds can be held responsible
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2 allows a broker to delegate supervisory tasks to another qualified license holder, but that delegation does not transfer away the broker's ultimate responsibility for ensuring adequate supervision -- particularly across multiple office locations, where the broker must confirm delegated reviews are actually happening, not merely assign the task and disengage; a delegation that exists on paper only does not satisfy the broker's own non-delegable responsibility.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- delegation and multi-office supervision); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A buyer's earnest money check, timely deposited by the broker within two business days as required, bounces for insufficient funds a week later. The broker learns of the NSF notice from the bank before either principal does. The broker's appropriate response is to:
choice_a: Promptly notify both the buyer's and seller's sides of the NSF check so the parties can address the resulting default under the contract's earnest money provisions, since failing to timely fund a required earnest money deposit -- including via a check that ultimately fails to clear -- can itself put the buyer in default, subject to any notice-and-cure procedure the contract provides
choice_b: Say nothing to either party and simply wait to see whether the buyer voluntarily replaces the funds before closing
choice_c: Treat the bounced check as the broker's own problem to quietly resolve by covering the shortfall personally without telling the principals
choice_d: Automatically terminate the contract on the buyer's behalf the moment the NSF notice arrives, without regard to any cure period the contract may provide
explanation: A broker who learns that a deposited earnest money check has failed to clear must promptly inform the parties, since a valid, funded earnest money deposit is typically a material contractual obligation and a check that ultimately bounces can place the buyer in default under the contract's own earnest money provisions -- but the broker does not have independent authority to unilaterally declare a default or terminate the contract; that determination follows whatever process the contract itself specifies, including any required notice and opportunity to cure.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.146 (Maintaining Trust Money -- accounting to principals); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline V.A (Promulgated Contracts, Forms, and Addenda) and VII (Case Studies)

question: A brokerage's own listing is drawing strong interest, and two of the brokerage's own sponsored sales agents each separately represent a different buyer who wants to make an offer on that same listing. To properly proceed, the broker generally must:
choice_a: Recognize that the brokerage now represents the seller and both competing buyers in the same transaction, requiring written consent to intermediary status from all three principals, with each buyer's agent (and the listing agent) properly appointed to their respective party if appointments are used, so that each side still receives individual advice and advocacy through their own appointed agent
choice_b: Require one of the two buyer's agents to immediately stop representing their buyer, since a single brokerage can never simultaneously represent more than two principals in one transaction
choice_c: Simply let the two buyer's agents negotiate directly against each other with no special consent or appointment process, since they are not the listing agent
choice_d: Treat the situation as identical to any ordinary multiple-offer scenario requiring no additional consent beyond the original listing agreement
explanation: When a brokerage's own agents represent both the seller through the listing and more than one competing buyer on the same property, the brokerage represents every one of those parties in that single transaction -- intermediary status and written consent are required from all of them, and where appointments are used, each buyer's agent, along with the listing agent, can still be individually appointed to advise and advocate for their own assigned party, extending the same appointed-agent structure to a three-way (or more) in-house scenario rather than a simple two-sided one.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sections 1101.559-1101.561 (Intermediary Practice and Appointments); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)

question: A buyer properly delivers written notice terminating the contract during the option period, in exact compliance with the contract's termination procedure, and is contractually entitled to a full refund of earnest money. The seller nonetheless refuses to sign a Release of Earnest Money form, insisting -- incorrectly, based on the plain contract language -- that the buyer forfeited the deposit. The broker holding the funds should:
choice_a: Explain to the seller that the buyer's timely, proper option-period termination entitles the buyer to the earnest money under the contract's own terms, but still decline to unilaterally disburse the funds without a signed release from both parties (or another lawful basis, such as the contract's specified dispute-resolution process), since a broker may not act as final judge of a contested trust-fund claim even when one party's contractual position appears clear
choice_b: Immediately release the funds to the buyer without the seller's signature, since the broker has independently determined the buyer is correct
choice_c: Refuse to release the funds to either party indefinitely, with no further action, since any seller objection makes the matter permanently unresolvable
choice_d: Split the earnest money evenly between both parties as an easy compromise, regardless of what the contract actually provides
explanation: Even when the contract's plain language makes a party's entitlement to earnest money reasonably clear, a broker holding disputed trust funds is not the final arbiter of the parties' rights and generally may not disburse funds without a signed release from both principals or another lawful basis such as invoking the contract's dispute-resolution provision -- the broker's role is to correctly explain the parties' apparent contractual positions and press for a proper release or resolution, not to unilaterally decide the outcome and disburse based on the broker's own reading of the contract.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.652(b)(31); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline V.A (Promulgated Contracts, Forms, and Addenda -- option period) and VII (Case Studies)

question: During a periodic audit of closed transaction files, a broker discovers that over the past year, several intermediary transactions closed without a properly signed written consent-to-intermediary document in the file, even though the broker's records show the transactions otherwise proceeded as if consent had been obtained informally. Because these transactions are already closed, the broker's appropriate response is to:
choice_a: Recognize that missing consent cannot be meaningfully fixed retroactively for transactions that have already closed, and instead focus on documenting the audit finding, correcting the office's process and training going forward so future files are not affected, retaining the audit record itself, and consulting with legal counsel or the broker's E&O carrier about the potential exposure from the already-closed files
choice_b: Simply have the affected clients sign a consent form now, dated to reflect when the transaction actually closed, so the file appears complete
choice_c: Ignore the finding entirely, since the transactions already closed successfully with no client complaints
choice_d: Conclude that nothing further is required beyond correcting the agents' future paperwork habits, since past closed files carry no further significance once a transaction is complete
explanation: Consent to intermediary status must be obtained before the broker acts as intermediary; once a transaction has already closed without it, there is no way to genuinely go back and obtain valid contemporaneous consent, and backdating a document to make a file appear complete would itself be a serious integrity violation. The broker's realistic and appropriate response is a forward-looking corrective process paired with an honest reckoning -- through counsel and the broker's insurer -- of what exposure the already-closed files may carry, rather than either ignoring the problem or attempting to paper over it after the fact.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559 (Broker Acting as Intermediary); 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- recordkeeping); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline VII (Case Studies)
